```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

This article will briefly outline a strategy for writing plant breeding
program simulations in AlphaSimR using a very simple clonal breeding
program as an example. This example will model the breeding program for
20 years. The example will also generate plots to show the change in
mean genetic value and genetic variance over time for the first stage of
the breeding program.

Complete code for the simulation is provided after step 6. The steps
in-between demonstrate the process used to write this code. Note that
some intermediate steps provide invalid code, so you shouldn't run code
for the intermediate steps. Only run the final, complete code.

Step 7 then extends the simulation into the form most simulation
studies take: a burn-in period, alternative scenarios run from the same
burn-in, and replicates, with the results collected for comparison.

## 1. Translate program description to code

Begin by translating a description of the breeding program directly into
AlphaSimR code. Don't worry about whether or not the code runs just yet
and instead focus on making sure that the code is faithful
representation of the breeding program's description. This code will be
used later when you write code that will actually run.

### Breeding program description by year

#### Year 1 (Crossing)

Make 100 bi-parental crosses at random using all clones from Stage 2 and
Stage 3 yield trials as parents. The total number of parents will be 60.

#### Year 2 (Seedlings)

Grow out 10 seeds per bi-parental family for a total of 1000 F1
seedlings.

#### Year 3 (Stage 1)

Clonally propagate all seedlings for Stage 1 testing. Stage 1 testing is
performed using a single plot per clone and has a residual error
variance of 4.

#### Year 4 (Stage 2)

Select the best 50 clones from Stage 1 yield trial to advance to Stage
2. Stage 2 is performed using four replicate plots and has a residual
error variance of 4.

#### Year 5 (Stage 3)

Select the best 10 clones from Stage 2 to advance to Stage 3. Stage 3 is
performed using eight replicate plots and has a residual error variance
of 4.

### Description as code

```{r eval=FALSE}
# Year 1 (Crossing)
Parents = c(Stage2, Stage3)
F1 = randCross(Parents, nCrosses=100, nProgeny=10)

# Year 2 (Seedlings)
Seedlings = F1

# Year 3 (Stage 1)
Stage1 = setPheno(Seedlings, reps=1, varE=4)

# Year 4 (Stage 2)
Stage2 = selectInd(Stage1, nInd=50)
Stage2 = setPheno(Stage2, reps=4, varE=4)

# Year 5 (Stage 3)
Stage3 = selectInd(Stage2, nInd=10)
Stage3 = setPheno(Stage3, reps=8, varE=4)
```

## 2. Create founder haplotypes

This will be your first piece of executable code. I suggest using the
founder haplotypes to represent your initial parents, so you will need
60 individuals.

```{r eval=FALSE}
founderPop = runMacs(nInd=60, nChr=4, segSites=1000)
```

## 3. Set simulation parameters

We will only add a single trait to this simulation. The mean and
variance of this trait will represent the mean and variance of the
initial parents. Since there is no selection between crossing the
parents and growing Stage 1 clones, these values will also approximately
equal the mean and variance of the initial Stage 1 clones.

```{r eval=FALSE}
SP = SimParam$
  new(founderPop)$
  addTraitA(1000)
```

## 4. Fill breeding program pipeline

The purpose of this stage is to place unique individuals in every stage
of the breeding program. We don't want the exact same individuals to be
in multiple stages of the breeding program at the same time. We will
generate all individuals from the initial parents, so they won't have
the generational differences we'd expect in a real breeding program.
This generational difference will be created later in the simulation as
future years are simulated.

```{r eval=FALSE}
Parents = newPop(founderPop)

# Year 5 (Stage 3)
F1 = randCross(Parents, nCrosses=100, nProgeny=10)
Seedlings = F1
Stage1 = setPheno(Seedlings, reps=1, varE=4)
Stage2 = selectInd(Stage1, nInd=50)
Stage2 = setPheno(Stage2, reps=4, varE=4)
Stage3 = selectInd(Stage2, nInd=10)
Stage3 = setPheno(Stage3, reps=8, varE=4)

# Year 4 (Stage 2)
F1 = randCross(Parents, nCrosses=100, nProgeny=10)
Seedlings = F1
Stage1 = setPheno(Seedlings, reps=1, varE=4)
Stage2 = selectInd(Stage1, nInd=50)
Stage2 = setPheno(Stage2, reps=4, varE=4)

# Year 3 (Stage 1)
F1 = randCross(Parents, nCrosses=100, nProgeny=10)
Seedlings = F1
Stage1 = setPheno(Seedlings, reps=1, varE=4)

# Year 2 (Seedlings)
F1 = randCross(Parents, nCrosses=100, nProgeny=10)
Seedlings = F1

# Year 1 (Crossing)
F1 = randCross(Parents, nCrosses=100, nProgeny=10)
```

## 5. Simulate 20 years of breeding

This part of the script will model the breeding program in action. Thus,
you need to advance material as it would be advanced in a real breeding
program. This means you need to be careful not to delete or overwrite a
population you need later. The most efficient way of doing this is
usually to start at the final stage of the breeding program and work
your way toward earlier stages, because this often lets you avoid
making copies of populations.

```{r eval=FALSE}
for(year in 1:20){
  # Year 5 (Stage 3)
  Stage3 = selectInd(Stage2, nInd=10)
  Stage3 = setPheno(Stage3, reps=8, varE=4)
  
  # Year 4 (Stage 2)
  Stage2 = selectInd(Stage1, nInd=50)
  Stage2 = setPheno(Stage2, reps=4, varE=4)
  
  # Year 3 (Stage 1)
  Stage1 = setPheno(Seedlings, varE=4)
  
  # Year 2 (Seedlings)
  Seedlings = F1
  
  # Year 1 (Crossing)
  Parents = c(Stage3, Stage2)
  F1 = randCross(Parents, nCrosses=100, nProgeny=10)
}
```

## 6. Report results

I like to write code for reporting results at the end, but the code
itself often needs to occur within code you've already written. This is
the case in this simulation, because we are overwriting populations in
each new year. Thus, we must save summary data in each year.

First, we need to create a couple of vectors for storing the summary data.
This code needs to occur before simulating the 20 years of breeding.

```{r eval=FALSE}
meanStage1 = numeric(20)
varStage1 = numeric(20)
```

Then, the code for reporting the results needs to occur inside the loop
for simulating 20 years of breeding.

```{r eval=FALSE}
for(year in 1:20){
  # Code for advancing one year
  
  # Report mean and variance
  meanStage1[year] = meanG(Stage1)
  varStage1[year] = varG(Stage1)
}
```

Finally, here is the code for generating plots of the summary data. This
code occurs after the simulation is complete.

```{r eval=FALSE}
plot(1:20, meanStage1, type="l", xlab="Year", ylab="Mean", main="Mean Stage 1")
plot(1:20, varStage1, type="l", xlab="Year", ylab="Variance", main="Variance Stage 1")
```

## Full Code

```{r}
library(AlphaSimR)

## Create founder haplotypes
founderPop = runMacs(nInd=60, nChr=4, segSites=1000)

## Set simulation parameters
SP = SimParam$
  new(founderPop)$
  addTraitA(1000)

## Fill breeding program pipeline
Parents = newPop(founderPop)

# Year 5 (Stage 3)
F1 = randCross(Parents, nCrosses=100, nProgeny=10)
Seedlings = F1
Stage1 = setPheno(Seedlings, reps=1, varE=4)
Stage2 = selectInd(Stage1, nInd=50)
Stage2 = setPheno(Stage2, reps=4, varE=4)
Stage3 = selectInd(Stage2, nInd=10)
Stage3 = setPheno(Stage3, reps=8, varE=4)

# Year 4 (Stage 2)
F1 = randCross(Parents, nCrosses=100, nProgeny=10)
Seedlings = F1
Stage1 = setPheno(Seedlings, reps=1, varE=4)
Stage2 = selectInd(Stage1, nInd=50)
Stage2 = setPheno(Stage2, reps=4, varE=4)

# Year 3 (Stage 1)
F1 = randCross(Parents, nCrosses=100, nProgeny=10)
Seedlings = F1
Stage1 = setPheno(Seedlings, reps=1, varE=4)

# Year 2 (Seedlings)
F1 = randCross(Parents, nCrosses=100, nProgeny=10)
Seedlings = F1

# Year 1 (Crossing)
F1 = randCross(Parents, nCrosses=100, nProgeny=10)

## Create vectors for output
meanStage1 = numeric(20)
varStage1 = numeric(20)

## Simulate 20 years of breeding
for(year in 1:20){
  # Year 5 (Stage 3)
  Stage3 = selectInd(Stage2, nInd=10)
  Stage3 = setPheno(Stage3, reps=8, varE=4)
  
  # Year 4 (Stage 2)
  Stage2 = selectInd(Stage1, nInd=50)
  Stage2 = setPheno(Stage2, reps=4, varE=4)
  
  # Year 3 (Stage 1)
  Stage1 = setPheno(Seedlings, reps=1, varE=4)
  
  # Year 2 (Seedlings)
  Seedlings = F1
  
  # Year 1 (Crossing)
  Parents = c(Stage3, Stage2)
  F1 = randCross(Parents, nCrosses=100, nProgeny=10)
  
  # Report mean and variance
  meanStage1[year] = meanG(Stage1)
  varStage1[year] = varG(Stage1)
}

## Plot mean and variance
plot(1:20, meanStage1, type="l", xlab="Year", ylab="Mean", main="Mean Stage 1")
plot(1:20, varStage1, type="l", xlab="Year", ylab="Variance", main="Variance Stage 1")

```

## 7. Compare scenarios with a burn-in and replicates

A single run of a breeding program tells you little on its own. The
usual purpose of a simulation is to compare alternative versions of a
program, and that comparison needs three things the code above does not
have.

-   A **burn-in**: a period of breeding under the current program before
    the alternatives begin. The founders produced by `runMacs` have
    never been selected, so the first years of any program are atypical.
    The burn-in puts the program into a realistic state, and starting
    every scenario from the same burn-in means the scenarios differ only
    in what happens afterward.
-   **Scenarios**: the alternative programs being compared, each run
    forward from the end of the burn-in.
-   **Replicates**: independent repeats of the whole process, each with
    new founders and a new burn-in. A simulation is a random draw, so a
    difference between scenarios means nothing until you know how much
    it varies between replicates.

As an example, we will compare the program above with an alternative
that uses the same number of plots each year. The current program
tests 1000 Stage 1 clones in one plot each, 50 Stage 2 clones in four
plots each and 10 Stage 3 clones in eight plots each, for 1280 plots.
The alternative makes 80 crosses instead of 100, giving 800 Stage 1
clones, and spends the 200 plots this saves on testing Stage 2 clones in
eight plots each instead of four. It trades selection intensity in Stage
1 for accuracy in Stage 2. Keeping the number of plots equal is what
makes this a fair comparison: an alternative that simply tested more
material would win by spending more.

### A function for one year

When the same program is run under several settings, it is easier to
keep the populations in a list and write the year as a function. The
function below advances every stage by one year, exactly as the loop
above does, with the number of crosses and the number of Stage 2 plots
as arguments. It also returns the number of plots used, so that the
cost of each scenario is recorded rather than assumed.

```{r}
library(AlphaSimR)

runYear = function(prog, nCrosses, nRepStage2){
  # Year 5 (Stage 3)
  prog$Stage3 = selectInd(prog$Stage2, nInd=10)
  prog$Stage3 = setPheno(prog$Stage3, reps=8, varE=4)

  # Year 4 (Stage 2)
  prog$Stage2 = selectInd(prog$Stage1, nInd=50)
  prog$Stage2 = setPheno(prog$Stage2, reps=nRepStage2, varE=4)

  # Year 3 (Stage 1)
  prog$Stage1 = setPheno(prog$Seedlings, reps=1, varE=4)

  # Year 2 (Seedlings)
  prog$Seedlings = prog$F1

  # Year 1 (Crossing)
  prog$F1 = randCross(c(prog$Stage3, prog$Stage2),
                      nCrosses=nCrosses, nProgeny=10)

  # Plots used this year across the three yield trial stages
  prog$nPlots = nInd(prog$Stage1) +
    nRepStage2*nInd(prog$Stage2) +
    8*nInd(prog$Stage3)
  return(prog)
}
```

The functions called inside `runYear` find the simulation parameters by
looking for an object called `SP` in the global environment, so `SP`
must be created there, as it is below, or passed to each function
through its `simParam` argument.

### Scenarios within replicates

Each replicate creates new founders, fills the pipeline, runs a burn-in
of 10 years under the current program, and then runs each scenario for
10 more years from the state the burn-in left. The results are collected
as one row per replicate, scenario and year, which is the most
convenient form for summarizing and plotting later. Year 0 records the
end of the burn-in, which every scenario in a replicate shares.

```{r}
set.seed(1234)

nReps = 5
nBurnin = 10
nFuture = 10
scenarios = list(
  Current = list(nCrosses=100, nRepStage2=4),
  Alternative = list(nCrosses=80, nRepStage2=8)
)

results = list()
for(rep in 1:nReps){
  ## New founders and simulation parameters for each replicate
  founderPop = runMacs(nInd=60, nChr=4, segSites=1000)
  SP = SimParam$
    new(founderPop)$
    addTraitA(1000)

  ## Fill breeding program pipeline, as in step 4
  Parents = newPop(founderPop)
  prog = list()

  # Year 5 (Stage 3)
  Stage1 = setPheno(randCross(Parents, nCrosses=100, nProgeny=10),
                    reps=1, varE=4)
  Stage2 = setPheno(selectInd(Stage1, nInd=50), reps=4, varE=4)
  prog$Stage3 = setPheno(selectInd(Stage2, nInd=10), reps=8, varE=4)

  # Year 4 (Stage 2)
  Stage1 = setPheno(randCross(Parents, nCrosses=100, nProgeny=10),
                    reps=1, varE=4)
  prog$Stage2 = setPheno(selectInd(Stage1, nInd=50), reps=4, varE=4)

  # Year 3 (Stage 1)
  prog$Stage1 = setPheno(randCross(Parents, nCrosses=100, nProgeny=10),
                         reps=1, varE=4)

  # Year 2 (Seedlings)
  prog$Seedlings = randCross(Parents, nCrosses=100, nProgeny=10)

  # Year 1 (Crossing)
  prog$F1 = randCross(Parents, nCrosses=100, nProgeny=10)

  ## Burn-in under the current program
  for(year in 1:nBurnin){
    prog = runYear(prog, nCrosses=100, nRepStage2=4)
  }
  burnin = prog

  ## Run each scenario forward from the same burn-in
  for(scenario in names(scenarios)){
    prog = burnin
    settings = scenarios[[scenario]]
    for(year in 0:nFuture){
      if(year > 0){
        prog = runYear(prog, nCrosses=settings$nCrosses,
                       nRepStage2=settings$nRepStage2)
      }
      results[[length(results) + 1]] = data.frame(
        rep = rep,
        scenario = scenario,
        year = year,
        meanG = unname(meanG(prog$Stage1)),
        varG = c(varG(prog$Stage1)),
        nPlots = if(year > 0) prog$nPlots else NA
      )
    }
  }
}
results = do.call(rbind, results)
head(results)
```

Copying `burnin` into `prog` before each scenario works because
populations are ordinary R objects: changing `prog` leaves `burnin`
untouched. `SP` is different. It is an R6 object with reference
semantics, so every scenario shares the same one, and anything a
scenario changes in it, such as the error variance set with
`SP$setVarE()`, carries over into the scenarios run after it. Sharing it
is safe here because no scenario changes it; the only state it
accumulates is the counter used to assign IDs, which keeps IDs unique
across scenarios. When scenarios do change the simulation parameters, or
when they are run as separate jobs, save the burn-in to a file and have
each scenario load its own copy.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# At the end of the burn-in
saveRDS(list(prog=prog, SP=SP), paste0("burnin_", rep, ".rds"))

# At the start of each scenario
burnin = readRDS(paste0("burnin_", rep, ".rds"))
prog = burnin$prog
SP = burnin$SP
```

### Summarize the results

First, check that the scenarios really did cost the same. The years
just after the burn-in are a transition, because the pipeline still
holds material from the old program, so look at the last year.

```{r}
aggregate(nPlots ~ scenario, data=results[results$year == nFuture, ],
          FUN=mean)
```

Genetic gain is measured from the end of the burn-in, so the starting
level of each replicate, which varies with its founders, drops out. The
two scenarios match for the first two years, because Stage 1 then still
holds clones from crosses made during the burn-in.

```{r fig.width=6, fig.height=4.5}
start = results[results$year == 0, c("rep", "scenario", "meanG")]
names(start)[3] = "startG"
results = merge(results, start)
results$gain = results$meanG - results$startG

avgGain = aggregate(gain ~ scenario + year, data=results, FUN=mean)
plot(gain ~ year, data=avgGain[avgGain$scenario == "Current", ],
     type="l", ylim=range(avgGain$gain), xlab="Year after burn-in",
     ylab="Gain in mean genetic value", main="Stage 1")
lines(gain ~ year, data=avgGain[avgGain$scenario == "Alternative", ],
      lty=2)
legend("bottomright", legend=c("Current", "Alternative"), lty=1:2)
```

The scenarios in each replicate share a burn-in, so compare them within
replicates. Taking the difference in final gain for each replicate and
summarizing those differences removes the variation that comes from the
founders and gives a much more precise comparison than the two averages
alone.

```{r}
final = results[results$year == nFuture, ]
final = final[order(final$rep), ]
diffGain = final$gain[final$scenario == "Alternative"] -
  final$gain[final$scenario == "Current"]
c(mean=mean(diffGain), se=sd(diffGain)/sqrt(nReps))
```

Five replicates keep this article quick to build, but they are too few
for a reliable conclusion. A real study would use enough replicates for
the standard error of the difference to be small next to the difference
itself, and would look at the genetic variance in `results` as well as
the gain, because a scenario that gains faster by using up genetic
variance may fall behind over a longer horizon.

## Miscellaneous comments

You can write chunks of code as R scripts and call one script from
another using the `source` function. I typically do this to modularize
my code. I rarely write a simulation as single script, as shown in this
example.

You may also consider defining your own functions to produce tidier
code. See this help document for an example of how to write a function:

```{r eval=FALSE}
?`function`
```

A convenient way to avoid overwriting populations is saving them to a
list. This requires more memory and makes coding a bit more complicated,
so I rarely use this approach. However, it does let you save all data
from your simulation which can come in handy when you forget to measure
something that you realize you need later. Below is a brief
demonstration:

```{r}
library(AlphaSimR)

founderPop = quickHaplo(nInd=50, nChr=4, segSites=1000, inbred=TRUE)

SP = SimParam$
  new(founderPop)$
  addTraitA(1000)

Parents = newPop(founderPop)

# Create list for generations F1 through F10
Pop = vector("list", 10) 

# Produce F1s from a random biparental cross
Pop[[1]] = randCross(Parents, nCrosses=1, nProgeny=1000) 

# Produce F2 through F10 generations using selfing
for(i in 2:10){
  Pop[[i]] = self(Pop[[i-1]]) 
}

# Calculate genetic variance by generation
lapply(Pop, varG) 
```
